text: Open with a claim, not a definition Take the question "Examine the impact of urbanization on Indian cities". Most answers start by explaining what urbanization means. The examiner already knows. In the topper copies we studied, the strongest openings take a position on the question in the first sentence. They do not define the term. Two or three numbers, not twenty A claim with nothing behind it reads weak. A claim with one well-chosen number reads strong. Toppers use two or three data points per answer and pick the one that makes the point. Instead of memorising 20 statistics per subject, pick three or four you can reuse across many questions. https://upscprepnotes.in/content/how-to-write-upsc-mains-answers?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel&utm_campaign=tip

The 7-minute answer You get about 7 minutes per Mains answer. Toppers used them like this: First minute: read the question twice, underline the demand, pick an angle. Next five: write without stopping. Last minute: underline key terms, add a diagram if it helps, close with a sentence. People who run out of time usually started writing before they knew what to say. https://upscprepnotes.in/content/how-to-write-upsc-mains-answers?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel&utm_campaign=tip

Short paragraphs get read The best answers keep paragraphs to three to five sentences, sometimes two. Long paragraphs get skimmed. Short ones make the examiner read every line. Underline the key term in a sentence, just the word, not the whole line. It sends the eye where you want it. https://upscprepnotes.in/content/how-to-write-upsc-mains-answers?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel&utm_campaign=tip

Write one answer a day, then review it Writing three or four answers a day does not help if you never compare them with a good one. For two weeks, write one answer a day.
